meta.title: The Salary Dossier
meta.subtitle: 15 moves for every side of a compensation conversation
meta.description: From pre-conversation research to closing the last gap — a closed-file reference for candidates, employees, and managers who know that money conversations are won before the room goes quiet.
meta.author: AI

cards.title: Know Your Market Number Before You Walk In
cards.hook: Walking in without a market number is walking in blind. They already know what the role pays.
cards.truth:
The person across from you researched the number. You should too.
• Pull pay data from at least three sources — Glassdoor, LinkedIn Salary, Levels.fyi.
• Knowing the range shifts what number you say with confidence.
• The trap: using one source. Ranges vary 20–40% by source and city.
cards.remember: Find out what the job pays before you ask for anything.
cards.theySee: A candidate sitting across the table who names a specific number with no hesitation.

signals.t: They agree quickly — your number landed inside their range.
They pivot to benefits — your salary ask may have hit their ceiling.
You named a number above what they expected — hold still.
They come back lower — that is the negotiation starting, not ending.

steps.title: Pull three data points
steps.desc: Check Glassdoor, LinkedIn Salary, and one industry report for the exact job title and city. Write down the midpoint.

steps.title: Adjust up for experience
steps.desc: If your experience exceeds the job description by three or more years, add 10–15% to the midpoint. Write that number.

steps.title: Pick one target number
steps.desc: Write down one specific dollar figure — not a range. You will open higher than this in the room.

cards.script: "Based on market data for this role in [city], I'm targeting [X]."
cards.counter:
When someone uses your ignorance of market rates to lowball you, you will see it this way.
• They offer a number fast with no range given — that is a lowball in disguise.
• Ask: "What's the full pay band for this level?"
• Check their offer against three public sources before responding.
cards.insight: Market data gets you into the room with confidence — the harder part is knowing whether to name your number first or wait for them to go.

cards.title: Decide Your Walk-Away Number Before the Conversation
cards.hook: Most people decide what is enough mid-conversation. That is where they get talked into less.
cards.truth:
Without a hard floor set in advance, the pressure of the room moves it.
• A walk-away number, set cold, resists in-room pressure and flattery.
• Once you name it silently to yourself, leaving gets easier than caving.
• The trap: setting the floor too low because you are grateful to be there.
cards.remember: Set the lowest number you will accept before you sit down.
cards.theySee: A person who pauses before answering, then gives a firm answer instead of folding.

signals.t: They compliment your skills before naming a number — expect a lower offer to follow.
They delay giving a number — buying time to read your reaction first.
They move up in small amounts — testing how little they can give before you stop pushing.
They say they need an answer today — pressure designed to skip your floor check.

steps.title: Write down your floor
steps.desc: Before any conversation, write the lowest number you will accept and still feel okay about in six months.

steps.title: Name your best option if this fails
steps.desc: Write down the specific job, rate, or offer you would take if this one falls through. Be honest about what it actually is.

steps.title: Say no out loud once
steps.desc: Say out loud before the meeting: 'That doesn't work for me. I need [X].' Practice it so it comes out flat, not apologetic.

cards.script: "I need to be at [X] to make this work. Is there room to get there?"
cards.counter:
When someone tries to move your floor during the conversation, you will feel it.
• They reference your current pay or your financial need — ignore it, return to your number.
• Say: "That's not where I need to land. My number is [X]."
• If they cannot reach your floor, leave. The floor is set. Don't renegotiate it.
cards.insight: The walk-away number only works if you actually walk — most people discover mid-conversation that they set it as a bluff, and that is when it costs them.

cards.title: Don't Volunteer Your Current Salary
cards.hook: Your current salary anchors their offer before you say anything else. Give it up and the negotiation starts from there.
cards.truth:
What you make now has nothing to do with what this role is worth. They know that — do you?
• Your current pay caps their offer before the conversation starts.
• Once you say it, you cannot unsay it — the number sits in the room.
• The trap: thinking transparency builds goodwill. It doesn't. It hands them a ceiling.
cards.remember: Your current salary is their tool, not yours. Keep it.
cards.theySee: A candidate who says 'I'd rather focus on what this role is worth in the market' instead of answering the direct question.

signals.t: They ask for your current salary early — they want to anchor low before you anchor high.
The application has a salary history field — leave it blank or write 'open to discussion'.
They mention what others in the role make — trying to anchor you to that number.
They look surprised at your target number — either it is above budget or above what they expected you to say.

steps.title: Prepare the deflection line
steps.desc: Write and say this today: 'I'd prefer to focus on the scope of the role and what it's worth in the market.' Say it flat, no apology.

steps.title: Check your state's law
steps.desc: Many US states ban employers from asking about salary history. Look up your state before the meeting so you know your rights.

steps.title: Redirect to market rate
steps.desc: If they push hard, name your target number — not your current one. 'I'm targeting [X] based on market data for this role.'

cards.script: "I'd rather not anchor to what I've made in the past — I'm focused on what this role is worth in the market."
cards.counter:
When someone uses your current salary to cap your ask, redirect immediately.
• They repeat your current salary back to you as a reference point — don't accept that frame.
• Say: "Past pay isn't the benchmark. What's the band for this role?"
• Refuse to let past pay define what this job is worth. They are two separate conversations.
cards.insight: In states where salary history questions are still legal, refusing to answer is an option — but silence has its own cost, and the next card covers how to manage going first without giving ground.

cards.title: Let Them Name a Number First When You Can
cards.hook: The first number in the room becomes the center of gravity for everything that follows. Make sure it is not a bad one.
cards.truth:
Whoever names a number first sets the range that everything else gets measured against.
• If they go first and it is high, you win. If low, you counter from their number.
• Either way, you start from their position — not from nothing.
• The trap: silence feels awkward, so most people name their number first to fill it.
cards.remember: Let them say a number first. Either way, you learn something.
cards.theySee: A candidate who shrugs slightly and asks 'What does this role pay?' instead of naming a figure.

signals.t: They name a number above your target — don't say yes immediately, negotiate upward.
They name a number below your floor — counter immediately, don't deliberate out loud.
They give a range — your number should land at or above the top of it.
They push the question back to you — they may not have authority or they want you to anchor yourself.

steps.title: Ask the direct question
steps.desc: Say: 'What's the salary range budgeted for this role?' Most hiring managers will answer if you ask plainly.

steps.title: Hold the silence after asking
steps.desc: After asking, stop talking. Count to five in your head. Let them fill the quiet. Do not rescue them.

steps.title: React to what you hear
steps.desc: If their number is high, negotiate up from it. If it is low, counter immediately. Never accept the first number given.

cards.script: "What's the salary range you have budgeted for this position?"
cards.counter:
When someone waits for you to name a number first so they can use it as an anchor against you.
• They ask 'What are you looking for?' before giving any context — deflect it.
• Say: "I'd love to hear the range first. Can you share it?"
• If they won't share a range, open 15–20% above your target to give yourself room.
cards.insight: Sometimes they genuinely don't know the range yet — which means the number you name first becomes the budget. That is its own kind of upper hand, and the next card shows how to use it.

cards.title: Read the Silence After You Name Your Number
cards.hook: The second after you say your number, they react — even if they say nothing. That pause is data.
cards.truth:
Silence after a number is not discomfort — it is calculation. Read it, don't fill it.
• A long pause means your number surprised them — up or down, you will know which direction fast.
• Filling the silence yourself undercuts your number before they have responded.
• The trap: talking yourself down in real time because quiet feels like rejection.
cards.remember: After you name your number, stop talking and watch what happens.
cards.theySee: A candidate sitting quietly with a small nod after naming a salary figure, making no sound and no explanation.

signals.t: They pick up a pen or look at notes — they are recording, which means they are considering.
They look away for a moment — they are running the math in their head.
They say 'interesting' or 'let me check on that' — your number is in range or above it.
They counter without pausing — they have a hard ceiling and your number hit it.

steps.title: Name your number cleanly
steps.desc: Say the number once with nothing after it. 'I'm targeting [X].' Full stop. No explanation, no softener.

steps.title: Count to seven silently
steps.desc: After you speak, hold the silence for at least seven seconds. Count in your head. Don't explain, don't fill it.

steps.title: Note their first reaction
steps.desc: Write down what they did in the silence — looked away, reached for paper, frowned, nodded. That is your read for the next move.

cards.counter:
When someone uses silence after your number to pressure you into explaining yourself.
• Your instinct is to soften the number — that is the trap. Don't.
• Say nothing extra. If five seconds pass, say: "Does that work with the range?"
• Silence from them is not a no. Wait for actual words before adjusting anything.
cards.insight: The instinct to fill silence is almost universal — which means the person who holds it longest usually gets the better number, and most people never once practice sitting in it.

cards.title: Anchor High, Then Give Ground on Purpose
cards.hook: The number you name first doesn't have to be your final number. It just has to be high enough that your real number looks reasonable by comparison.
cards.truth:
People don't judge offers against reality — they judge them against the first number they heard.
• Name 15–25% above your target. Let them negotiate down to where you wanted.
• They feel like they won. You get what you planned.
• The trap: anchoring so high it breaks credibility. Stay within the defensible range.
cards.remember: Open high so your real number looks like a fair deal.
cards.theySee: A hiring manager who nods and then proposes a counter that lands right at the candidate's actual target number.

signals.t: Their counter is exactly where you wanted — the anchor worked.
They seem annoyed — your anchor was too high. Adjust down to something defensible.
They ask how you landed on that number — have a market data source ready to name.
They accept or say they'll 'check' — you may have left money in the room. Note it.

steps.title: Set your anchor number
steps.desc: Add 15–25% to your real target. Write this number before the meeting. This is your opening figure.

steps.title: Back it with one data point
steps.desc: Have one sentence ready: 'Market data for this title in [city] puts the range at [X] to [Y].' Say it once.

steps.title: Give ground deliberately
steps.desc: When they counter below your anchor, move toward your real target — not lower. Stop there and hold.

cards.script: "Based on the scope of the role and market data, I'm targeting [anchor number]."
cards.counter:
When someone anchors high to pull your counter away from what they would actually accept.
• Notice they named a very specific high number fast — that is a planned anchor.
• Don't counter their anchor. Name your own number instead.
• Say: "I appreciate that. My number is [X]. Can we work from there?"
cards.insight: Anchoring high works until your anchor is so far from market that they stop taking you seriously — the real skill is knowing exactly where that ceiling sits, and most people only find it by going too far once.

cards.title: Give a Range Where Your Floor Is Their Ceiling
cards.hook: When asked for a range, most people put their target in the middle. That is how they end up with the bottom half.
cards.truth:
They hear the bottom of your range as your real number — so make the bottom your actual target.
• Name a range: low end is your floor, high end is your anchor.
• They negotiate toward the bottom — which is exactly where you wanted to land.
• The trap: real target in the middle means you take the lower end when they push.
cards.remember: Set your floor as the bottom of any range you state.
cards.theySee: A recruiter who offers the bottom of the candidate's stated range, feeling like they made a fair deal.

signals.t: They offer the low end of your range — that was your target, so you are exactly where you wanted.
They offer the midpoint of your range — you got more than your floor.
Rare: they come in above your high end — accept or anchor higher next round.
They say the top is too high — come down to the midpoint, still above your floor.

steps.title: Set your floor as range bottom
steps.desc: Decide your actual target number today. That becomes the bottom of the range you state out loud.

steps.title: Set the anchor at the top
steps.desc: Add 15–20% to your floor. That is the top of your stated range. You are fine landing anywhere inside it.

steps.title: State the range cleanly
steps.desc: Say: 'I'm looking at [floor] to [top].' No explanation needed after that. Let them respond.

cards.script: "I'm looking at [floor] to [top], depending on the full scope of the role."
cards.counter:
When someone gives you a range and you assume the midpoint is their target — it probably isn't.
• Assume the low end of their range is where they plan to land.
• Counter above their midpoint, not at it.
• Say: "Given the scope, I expect to land at the top of that range."
cards.insight: The range trick works once — after the first offer lands at your floor, the next negotiation starts from that number, so you need a new anchor each time the conversation reopens.

cards.title: When They Say That's Not in the Budget
cards.hook: 'That's not in the budget' is a position, not a fact. Treat it as the opening move it is.
cards.truth:
Budget limits are almost always softer than they sound. The word 'budget' is cover for 'we don't want to go there yet.'
• Naming the constraint back to them turns it into a conversation instead of a wall.
• They feel heard, lower their guard, and often reveal the real ceiling.
• The trap: accepting 'budget' as final. It is almost always a test of how hard you will push.
cards.remember: Say the budget problem back to them before pushing forward.
cards.theySee: A hiring manager who expected pushback but instead hears their concern reflected back at them, then visibly relaxes.

signals.t: They say 'budget' but don't give a hard number — there is room to move.
You reflect the constraint back and they pause — they are reconsidering or about to reveal more.
They pivot to benefits instead of money — the base is close to its real ceiling.
They say 'let me check with my manager' — the ceiling is higher than they showed you.

steps.title: Label the constraint
steps.desc: Say: 'It sounds like the budget is tighter than you'd like here.' Then stop. Let them respond. Don't fill the pause.

steps.title: Ask what's possible
steps.desc: Say: 'What's the most the role can get to?' Don't assume they have shown you the actual ceiling yet.

steps.title: Counter with one specific ask
steps.desc: If the base is genuinely frozen, ask for one thing in writing: a sign-on bonus, an earlier review date, or extra days off.

cards.script: "It sounds like the budget is tighter than you'd like on this. What's the most you can get the role to?"
cards.counter:
When someone uses your sympathy for their budget problem to stop you from pushing further.
• They name the budget limit before you have made your full ask — that is early pressure.
• Don't lower your number. Say: "What flexibility is there if the right person walks in?"
• Treat every 'no budget' as 'not yet' until you see a hard ceiling in writing.
cards.insight: The label works because people want to feel understood more than they want to hold a line — but if they have genuinely hit the ceiling, the label will reveal it fast, and then the conversation shifts to what else is on the table.

cards.title: When They Offer Perks Instead of Base Pay
cards.hook: Flexible hours and extra vacation days are nice. They don't show up on your W-2.
cards.truth:
They offer perks when the base is near its ceiling — it is a trade designed to feel like a win.
• Perks feel good in the moment but don't raise your starting point for the next negotiation.
• Your base pay sets the floor for every future raise, bonus, and counteroffer you will ever get.
• The trap: taking perks and calling it a win. Your future base starts where you accept today.
cards.remember: Base pay raises every future number. Perks do not.
cards.theySee: A candidate nodding at the perk offer, then pivoting directly back to a specific base number.

signals.t: They move from money to perks mid-conversation — the base is near its ceiling.
They spend more time on perks than pay — hoping you trade the number for the lifestyle.
They add remote flexibility when you push on base — it is a sweetener, not a raise.
They offer a better title with no money attached — titles don't pay bills.

steps.title: Name what you heard
steps.desc: Say: 'I appreciate the flexibility. I want to make sure we also close the gap on base.' Keep both in play at once.

steps.title: Put a dollar figure on each perk
steps.desc: Extra week of vacation at your daily rate equals [X]. Remote work saves [Y] in commute per month. Write it down.

steps.title: Make a specific trade if the math works
steps.desc: If the perk is worth enough, offer the trade explicitly. 'If I give up the extra week, can we get to [X] on base?'

cards.script: "I value that — and I want to close the base closer to [X]. Is there room to move there?"
cards.counter:
If someone uses perks to pull your attention away from a low base offer, notice the pattern.
• They brighten when you react positively to a perk — stay flat, return to base.
• Say: "I appreciate the flexibility. The base still needs to get to [X]."
• Don't let the perk conversation close before the base conversation does.
cards.insight: The harder move is valuing perks accurately and trading them deliberately — most people either reject perks entirely or take them without knowing what they gave up in base.

cards.title: When They Say They'll Circle Back on the Number
cards.hook: 'We'll revisit this in six months' means six months of working at the wrong number. Get the commitment now or put a date on it.
cards.truth:
Vague promises about future pay reviews disappear unless you tie them to something hard.
• A review date without a written benchmark is a verbal promise that resets every quarter.
• Naming a specific number and a specific date creates a real commitment, not an intention.
• The trap: accepting 'we'll revisit' and starting from zero six months later.
cards.remember: A pay review without a written benchmark is not a commitment.
cards.theySee: A manager who just said 'we'll circle back' and now faces a direct question about what that actually means in writing.

signals.t: They say 'soon' or 'next cycle' with no date — that is not a plan, it is a delay.
They tie the future review to performance with no named metric — that is a movable target.
They agree to a date fast — they know they owe you a real conversation.
They resist putting the review date in writing — the promise was not serious.

steps.title: Name the date out loud
steps.desc: Say: 'Can we set the review for [specific date] — 90 days from today?' A date forces a real commitment instead of an intention.

steps.title: Name the number tied to the date
steps.desc: Say: 'At that review, I'm expecting we'll get to [X]. Does that align with what you're planning?'

steps.title: Send a follow-up email that day
steps.desc: Same day, email: 'Per our conversation, we agreed to revisit my base on [date] with a target of [X].' That email is the record.

cards.script: "Let's set a firm date for that — can we put [90 days from today] on the calendar now, with a target of [X]?"
cards.counter:
When someone uses 'circle back' to close the conversation without giving you anything real.
• They say 'circle back' right after you push — that closes the push, not honors it.
• Say: "Can we put a specific date and number on that now?"
• If they won't commit to a date, the promise was never real.
cards.insight: The follow-up email you send that same day is worth more than the conversation itself — it is the only version of the promise that has a chance of surviving the next quarter.

cards.title: When a High Performer Can't Get a Raise Right Now
cards.hook: Telling your best person 'not right now' without a plan is how you hand them to a competitor. Give them a path or they will make their own.
cards.truth:
High performers weigh 'not now' against what they can get somewhere else — and they have options.
• Name the specific reason: budget cap, pay band ceiling, or timeline. Vague reasons read as excuses.
• Offer something concrete: a project, a title, a written review date with a target number.
• The trap: warm sympathy with no specifics. They will decide to quit easily.
cards.remember: Say exactly why. Then give them one concrete thing to reach.
cards.theySee: A manager who explains the specific pay band ceiling and then hands over a written review date with a target number attached to it.

signals.t: They show no reaction — they are already processing their options, not your words.
They ask almost nothing — they have thought this through and your answer confirmed something.
They ask 'how long?' specifically — they are deciding whether to wait or leave.
They reference the market or another offer — this conversation just became urgent.

steps.title: Name the real reason
steps.desc: Say the specific reason: 'Your pay is at the top of the band for this level. The band doesn't move until your role moves up.'

steps.title: Offer a written date and number
steps.desc: Say: 'I want to put [date] on the calendar as the review date, with [X] as the target we are working toward.'

steps.title: Follow up in 30 days
steps.desc: Send a note 30 days later referencing the conversation. Shows the plan is real. Most managers never do this — and that is exactly why people leave.

cards.script: "Your pay is at the top of the band right now. Here's what has to change for that to move — and I want to set a date to revisit it."
cards.counter:
If you are on the receiving end of this conversation, here is how to read it.
• Vague reasons with no date — the plan isn't real. Press for specifics.
• Ask: "What would I need to hit to get to [X] by [date]?"
• If they can't answer, the raise is not coming. Update your resume.
cards.insight: The manager who follows up 30 days later is the one who keeps the person — and almost no managers remember to do it, which is why high performers keep leaving for someone who will.

cards.title: When the Employee Brings Up a Coworker's Pay
cards.hook: The second you explain or compare, you lose. Defending another person's salary is a fight you cannot win.
cards.truth:
Comparing pays is a trap with no good exit — every answer gives them more to push back on.
• You cannot discuss another employee's pay. Say that once, clearly, then move on.
• Redirect to their specific situation: their pay band, their performance, their path forward.
• The trap: justifying someone else's pay. That is not your job.
cards.principle: Greene: Law 4 — Say Less Than Necessary
cards.remember: Don't explain another person's pay. Redirect to theirs.
cards.theySee: A manager who says 'I can't speak to that' once and immediately pivots to the employee's specific numbers and next steps.

signals.t: They name a specific colleague — they have information and are testing what you will confirm.
They use the word 'fair' — they feel undervalued and want acknowledgment, not a comparison.
They give a number for the coworker — may be secondhand. Don't confirm or deny it.
Their tone rises or they lean forward — this is about recognition, not just money.

steps.title: Say the one thing you can say
steps.desc: Say: 'I can't discuss anyone else's compensation — that's confidential.' Say it once, then move forward immediately.

steps.title: Redirect to their numbers
steps.desc: Say: 'What I can tell you is where you sit in your own pay band and how that compares to market for your role.'

steps.title: Name one path forward
steps.desc: Give them one concrete next step: a review date, a project to lead, or the specific skill that opens the next pay band.

cards.script: "I can't speak to anyone else's pay — that's confidential. Here's where you sit and what the path looks like from here."
cards.counter:
If your manager uses this deflection to avoid a real conversation about your specific pay.
• They say 'I can't discuss that' and pivot to vague generalities — ask for specifics.
• Say: "I'm not asking about them. Where do I sit in my own band?"
• If they won't share your own band, escalate to HR.
cards.insight: Most employees raise a coworker's pay when they actually want to hear that they are valued — answering that real question matters more than the comparison, and most managers miss it entirely.

cards.title: When You're the Manager Delivering a Pay Freeze
cards.hook: A pay freeze with no explanation is a resignation letter handed back to you. How you deliver it determines whether they stay.
cards.truth:
People can accept bad news when you describe it as a shared situation with a named path out.
• Name the business reason specifically: a revenue drop, a budget cut, a company-wide policy.
• Tie their future pay to a specific milestone — not 'when things improve.'
• The trap: softening the news so much they leave unclear on whether this is permanent.
cards.remember: Say the bad news clearly. Then say exactly when it can change.
cards.theySee: A manager who states the freeze plainly, names the specific reason, and then gives a specific review date — not a vague promise.

signals.t: Their expression drops — they were not expecting this. Give them a moment before continuing.
They go quiet and ask nothing — processing, not agreement. Check in directly.
They ask if others are affected — they are checking whether this is targeted at them specifically.
They want the real reason. Have it ready and say it plainly in one sentence.

steps.title: Say the news first
steps.desc: Open with the fact: 'Effective [date], your base is frozen at [X].' Don't bury it after three minutes of preamble.

steps.title: Name the reason in one sentence
steps.desc: Say exactly why: revenue, budget, company-wide policy. One sentence. Do not over-explain or hedge.

steps.title: Name the recovery milestone
steps.desc: Say: 'When [specific thing] happens, this gets reviewed. I'll put a date on the calendar right now.'

cards.script: "Starting [date], your base is being frozen at [X]. Here's why, and here's the specific point where we review it."
cards.counter:
If your manager is delivering bad pay news, read the delivery carefully.
• If they don't name a specific reason, ask: "What specifically triggered this?"
• If there's no recovery milestone, ask: "When can we set a review date?"
• If only you are affected with no reason given, document the conversation.
cards.insight: People forgive bad news faster than they forgive being misled — the manager who delivers it plainly is the one who keeps the team, and that gap in behavior is wider than most managers realize.

cards.title: Get the Offer in Writing Before You Say Yes
cards.hook: Verbal offers disappear. Job titles change. Start dates slip. The offer isn't real until it's in a document.
cards.truth:
Accepting verbally before the written offer creates the worst possible situation — you quit your last role and the new one changed.
• Verbal agreements are worth the air they are spoken into — get everything in writing.
• Review the written offer against what you negotiated: base, title, start date, bonus terms.
• The trap: feeling rude asking for it in writing. You're not rude. You're careful.
cards.remember: Don't say yes to anything until you see it written down.
cards.theySee: A recruiter who expected a yes right now but instead hears 'I'd love to review the written offer today.'

signals.t: They give numbers verbally but no written offer follows within 24 hours — ask for it.
They push you to commit to a start date before the offer letter is sent — hold the date.
The written offer is lower than what was said verbally — they are testing whether you will catch it.
They ask you to sign by end of day — read every line, don't rush.

steps.title: Ask for the written offer today
steps.desc: Say: 'Can you send the offer letter today so I can review everything?' This is normal. Do it every single time.

steps.title: Check against the verbal deal
steps.desc: Line up every number and term that was discussed against what the offer letter says. Mark anything that changed.

steps.title: Flag discrepancies before signing
steps.desc: If anything changed, say: 'The base here shows [X] — we discussed [Y]. Can you confirm which is correct?'

cards.script: "Can you send the written offer today? I want to make sure everything we discussed is captured before I sign."
cards.counter:
When someone uses urgency to get you to accept before you can review the full document.
• They pressure you to decide before a written document exists — that is a red flag.
• Say: "I need the written offer in hand before I accept. Send it today."
• If they say the offer can't wait, the problem is them, not your timeline.
cards.insight: The gap between the verbal offer and the written one is where the negotiation actually ends — and most people never check it, which is why it keeps happening to the same people twice.

cards.title: When the Number Is Close but Not Quite Right
cards.hook: They are at [X] and you need [Y]. The gap is small. One more push at the finish line is worth more than it feels right now.
cards.truth:
A small gap at the end of a long negotiation feels harder to close than it actually is — everyone is tired.
• One calibrated question at the finish line can move 3–5% with almost no friction.
• You have already done the hard work of getting here. The final ask costs almost nothing.
• The trap: accepting 'close enough' when the gap is still real money over years.
cards.remember: Ask one more question at the finish line. Most people don't.
cards.theySee: A recruiter who thought the deal was done, now facing one more direct question about the final gap before anyone signs anything.

signals.t: They offer something close to your target — they want to close, which means you have one move left.
They sound relieved — they expected more pushback and didn't get it. Use that.
They mention needing to wrap today — urgency works both ways.
The difference is less than 5% — a single question can close it.

steps.title: Name the gap precisely
steps.desc: Say: 'We're [exact dollar amount] apart. I want to close that.' Name the number, not a percentage.

steps.title: Ask the calibrated question
steps.desc: Say: 'What would it take to get there?' Then stop talking. Let them answer. Don't fill the silence.

steps.title: Accept or hold your floor
steps.desc: If they close the gap, say yes. If they can't, check whether the full package clears your walk-away number from Card 2. If yes, take it.

cards.script: "We're [gap] apart — is there any way to close that before we finish?"
cards.counter:
When someone uses the 'almost there' moment to get you to stop pushing.
• They sigh and say 'we're so close' — that means they can still move.
• Hold your number. Say: "I know. Let's close the gap and then we're done."
• If they genuinely can't move, you will know fast. If they can, the question gets it.
cards.insight: The difference between [X] and [Y] over three years is larger than it sounds in the room — and the person who asks one more question last usually gets closer to what they wanted, simply because everyone else stopped asking.
